== Biography ==

Cotton-tail is one of four young rabbits dwelling in a sand-bank beneath the root of a very big fir-tree, where they live with their Mother. A good little bunny by nature, Cotton-tail exhibits the quiet obedience and sensible disposition that one might hope to find in young rabbit-folk. This conduct stands in marked contrast to that of their sibling Peter, whose naughty inclinations lead him into considerable trouble.

With siblings Flopsy and Mopsy, Cotton-tail passes the days in wholesome pursuits, venturing down the lane to gather blackberries—a task both useful and agreeable to well-behaved young rabbits. When evening falls, Cotton-tail partakes of a modest supper of bread, milk, and the blackberries gathered during the day, a simple but nourishing meal earned through proper conduct.

== Narrative role ==

Cotton-tail is one of four young rabbits living with their mother in a sand-bank beneath the roots of a great fir-tree. The four siblings are named Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and [[Peter]]. Like Flopsy and Mopsy, Cotton-tail is described as a good little bunny.

When their mother went out one morning, Cotton-tail went down the lane with Mopsy to gather blackberries. This task was undertaken while Peter, in contrast to his more obedient siblings, made his way to Mr. [[McGregor]]'s garden in direct disobedience of their mother's wishes.

That evening, Cotton-tail took supper with Flopsy and Mopsy, enjoying bread, milk, and the blackberries they had gathered. The meal stood in contrast to Peter's experience that day: while his siblings enjoyed the fruits of their proper conduct, Peter lay in bed drinking camomile tea, suffering the consequences of his misbehavior.

== Personality ==

Cotton-tail is characterized as "a good little bunny," a phrase that names her defining traits: obedience and restraint. While her brother Peter is "very naughty" and transgresses, Cotton-tail demonstrates respect for her mother's guidance and the boundaries set for the family. She is inclined toward compliance, preferring permitted activities to ventures into forbidden territory. Her disposition earns her care and comfort—a wholesome supper of bread, milk, and blackberries—a reward that reflects her consistent virtue and respectful nature.

== Appearance ==

Cotton-tail is one of four little rabbit siblings—Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter—who make their home in a sand-bank beneath the root of a very large fir-tree. The four live with their mother, old Mrs. Rabbit, in this underground dwelling.

Cotton-tail is a good little bunny. One morning when their mother departed to visit the baker's, having prepared brown bread and currant buns for breakfast, Cotton-tail went with Flopsy and Mopsy down the lane to gather blackberries.

The day's work concluded with supper. Cotton-tail shared an evening meal with Flopsy and Mopsy of bread and milk accompanied by the blackberries they had gathered that day—a wholesome repast earned through honest labor.

Cotton-tail's household was governed by their mother's clear instructions. All four children were permitted to play in the fields or down the lane, but were forbidden from entering Mr. McGregor's garden. This boundary reflected a grave family history: their father had met with a dire accident there and had been made into a pie by Mrs. McGregor.

== Trivia ==

Cotton-tail is the third of four little rabbits dwelling in a sand-bank beneath the root of a great fir-tree. The siblings are Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter, and they live under the care of their Mother.

Cotton-tail is distinguished among the four as one of the good little bunnies. This virtue is demonstrated on the day recounted in the tale, when Cotton-tail chose to accompany Flopsy and Mopsy in gathering blackberries down the lane—a wholesome activity that their brother Peter spurned in favour of unauthorised entry into Mr. McGregor's garden.

The difference in temperament between Cotton-tail and Peter is reflected in the evening's events. While Peter, having been caught and pursued, returned home ill and was put to bed with camomile tea as remedy and consequence, Cotton-tail enjoyed a proper supper of bread and milk alongside the blackberries gathered during the day. The contrast between the siblings' fates reflects the virtue of obedience against the folly of disobedience.

As one of the good little rabbits, Cotton-tail represents the path of duty and the reward that follows from prudent behaviour, serving as counterpoint to Peter's cautionary tale of youthful imprudence.
